units.title: Fractions
units.subject: maths
national_curriculum_refs: Ma3/2.4a count up and down in tenths
Ma3/2.4b recognise, find and write fractions of a discrete set of objects
Ma3/2.4c recognise and use fractions as numbers: unit fractions and non-unit fractions with small denominators
Ma3/2.4d recognise and show, using diagrams, equivalent fractions with small denominators
Ma3/2.4e compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators
learning_objectives: Understand that a fraction describes equal parts of a whole
Name unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5) from diagrams and real objects
Find a unit fraction of a small quantity by sharing equally (e.g. 1/4 of 12)
Recognise that the larger the denominator, the smaller each equal part
Identify simple equivalent fractions using diagrams (e.g. 1/2 = 2/4)
Compare and order unit fractions and fractions with the same denominator

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks 1/4 is larger than 1/2 because 4 is larger than 2.
misconceptions.why: Pupils apply whole-number reasoning to denominators.
misconceptions.response: Use identical shapes (pizzas/chocolate bars) cut into 2 vs 4 equal parts; physically compare one piece from each.

misconceptions.misconception: Counts parts without checking they are equal.
misconceptions.why: The word 'parts' is taken to mean any parts, not equal parts.
misconceptions.response: Show a shape split into unequal parts and ask 'is the shaded bit really one third?'. Fold paper strips to prove equality.

misconceptions.misconception: Reads 3/4 as 'three and four' or 'three fours'.
misconceptions.why: Fraction notation is unfamiliar; the bar is ignored.
misconceptions.response: Model the language 'three quarters = 3 out of 4 equal parts'; link numerator to count, denominator to part-size.

misconceptions.misconception: Believes a fraction of a set must be a fraction, not a whole number.
misconceptions.why: Confusion between the fraction (operator) and the answer.
misconceptions.response: Share 12 counters into 4 equal groups; 1/4 of 12 = 3, a whole number.

lessons.title: Understanding the whole and equal parts
Finding a unit fraction of a quantity

baseline_questions: Shade 1/3 of a shape divided into 3 equal parts.
What fraction of these 4 stars is shaded? (1 shaded)
Find 1/4 of 8 counters.
Which is bigger: 1/2 or 1/5? Explain how you know.
Fill in the blank: 1/2 = ?/4
Write the fraction 'three quarters' using numbers.
Put these in order, smallest first: 1/2, 1/4, 1/3.

units.title: Addition and subtraction within 100
units.subject: maths
national_curriculum_refs: Ma2/2.2a solve problems with addition and subtraction using concrete objects and pictorial representations
Ma2/2.2b recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, derive related facts to 100
Ma2/2.2c add and subtract numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mentally
learning_objectives: Recall number bonds to 20 and derive bonds to 100
Add and subtract a two-digit number and ones
Add and subtract a two-digit number and tens
Recognise that addition can be done in any order but subtraction cannot
Use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction to check calculations

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks subtraction is commutative (24 - 6 same as 6 - 24).
misconceptions.why: Over-generalises the 'any order' rule from addition.
misconceptions.response: Use a number line and counters: you cannot take 24 away from 6. Model both directions.

misconceptions.misconception: Forgets to regroup (exchange) a ten when the ones digit is too small, e.g. 32 - 5 = 33.
misconceptions.why: Subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position.
misconceptions.response: Use base-ten blocks; exchange one ten for ten ones before subtracting.

misconceptions.misconception: Adds tens to ones, e.g. 34 + 20 = 36 or 54.
misconceptions.why: Place value of the added number is not tracked.
misconceptions.response: Partition: 34 + 20 -> 30 + 20 + 4. Use a hundred square to jump in tens.

prerequisites: Counting in tens from any number

lessons.title: Adding a two-digit number and ones

baseline_questions: What goes with 7 to make 20?
Work out 42 - 7 using regrouping.
Is 6 - 24 possible? Explain.
Check 45 + 23 = 68 using subtraction.
There are 27 apples. 40 more arrive. How many now?

units.title: Place value to 10,000
units.subject: maths
national_curriculum_refs: Ma4/2.1a count in multiples of 6, 7, 9, 25 and 1000
Ma4/2.1c recognise the place value of each digit in a four-digit number
Ma4/2.1d order and compare numbers beyond 1000
Ma4/2.1f round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000
learning_objectives: State the value of each digit in a four-digit number
Partition four-digit numbers in standard and non-standard ways
Compare and order numbers beyond 1000 using < > =
Round four-digit numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000
Count on and back in 1000s across boundaries

misconceptions.misconception: Reads 3046 as 'three hundred and forty-six' or ignores the zero.
misconceptions.why: Zero as a place holder is not understood.
misconceptions.response: Build the number with place-value counters and a place-value grid; discuss why the zero must stay.

misconceptions.misconception: Rounds 3450 to 3000 (rounds to nearest 1000 by looking at hundreds only, or 'rounds down when unsure').
misconceptions.why: The 'look at the next digit' rule is misapplied.
misconceptions.response: Use a number line marked in 1000s; mark 3450 and see which end it is closer to (3450 is halfway -> rounds up to 4000... check the digit being rounded).

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks a longer number is always larger without checking digits, e.g. compares 999 and 1000 correctly but 2999 and 3001 incorrectly.
misconceptions.why: Compares by counting digits, not by place value from the left.
misconceptions.response: Line numbers up in a place-value grid and compare from the highest column.

lessons.title: The value of each digit in a four-digit number

baseline_questions: What is the value of the 4 in 5423?
Partition 6207 into thousands, hundreds, tens and ones.
Round 3762 to the nearest 100.
Round 8500 to the nearest 1000.
1000 more than 4620 is ?
Order: 2999, 3010, 2909, 3100 (smallest first).

units.title: Multiplication and division (3, 4 and 8 times tables)
units.subject: maths
national_curriculum_refs: Ma3/2.3a recall and use multiplication and division facts for the 3, 4 and 8 multiplication tables
Ma3/2.3c solve problems, including missing number problems, involving multiplication and division
learning_objectives: Recall 3, 4 and 8 times-table facts
Understand multiplication as repeated addition and as arrays
Understand division as sharing and as grouping
Use the inverse relationship between multiplication and division
Solve missing-number problems (e.g. 4 x ? = 24)

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks division is commutative (12 / 3 = 3 / 12).
misconceptions.why: Transfers the 'any order' rule from multiplication.
misconceptions.response: Act out sharing 12 sweets between 3 people vs 3 sweets between 12 people.

misconceptions.misconception: Confuses the 4 and 8 times tables (doubles 4x once too few / too many times).
misconceptions.why: The 'double the 4s to get the 8s' shortcut is applied loosely.
misconceptions.response: Line up 4x and 8x arrays; show 8x is exactly double 4x for the same multiplier.

baseline_questions: Draw an array for 4 x 5.
Fill in: 4 x ? = 28.
Is 12 / 3 the same as 3 / 12? Explain.
There are 32 pencils shared equally into 8 pots. How many per pot?
Write a division fact from 6 x 4 = 24.

units.title: Writing a recount
units.subject: english
national_curriculum_refs: En3/3.1 plan writing by discussing and recording ideas
En3/3.2a use conjunctions, adverbs and prepositions to express time and cause
En3/3.3 proof-read for spelling and punctuation errors
learning_objectives: Sequence events in chronological order using time conjunctions (first, then, after that, finally)
Write in the past tense consistently
Write in the first person for a personal recount
Use paragraphs to group related events
Proof-read for full stops and capital letters

misconceptions.misconception: Slips between past and present tense within a sentence.
misconceptions.why: Narrating a vivid memory pulls the writer into the present.
misconceptions.response: Highlight every verb in one paragraph and check each is past tense; re-read aloud.

misconceptions.misconception: Writes one long sentence joined by 'and then ... and then'.
misconceptions.why: Spoken storytelling habits transfer to writing.
misconceptions.response: Give a bank of time conjunctions; rewrite a run-on sentence as three sentences.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks a recount needs an exciting made-up ending.
misconceptions.why: Confuses recount with narrative/story.
misconceptions.response: Compare a recount (what really happened) with a story; a recount ends with how you felt or a closing thought.

prerequisites: Forming sentences with capital letters and full stops
baseline_questions: List three time conjunctions you could use in a recount.
Rewrite in the past tense: 'I go to the park and I play football.'
Put these events in order: got home, woke up, ate breakfast, went to school.
Correct the punctuation: 'on saturday we went to the zoo we saw lions'
Write an opening sentence for a recount about a school trip.
Why does a recount use the first person?

units.title: Alternative graphemes for known phonemes
units.subject: english
national_curriculum_refs: En1/1 apply phonic knowledge and skills to decode words
En1/2 respond speedily with the correct sound to graphemes for all 40+ phonemes, including alternatives
learning_objectives: Blend sounds to read words containing taught GPCs
Recognise that one sound can be written in more than one way (ai / ay / a-e)
Read common exception words (the, said, one, was)
Segment spoken words into sounds for spelling

misconceptions.misconception: Sounds out every letter of a digraph separately (s-h-i-p as four sounds).
misconceptions.why: One-letter-one-sound expectation from early phonics.
misconceptions.response: Underline the digraph as one unit; use sound buttons with a bar under 'sh'.

misconceptions.misconception: Tries to sound out common exception words letter by letter (s-ai-d).
misconceptions.why: The decoding strategy is applied to non-decodable words.
misconceptions.response: Teach the tricky part explicitly; 'say the sounds you can, learn the bit that's odd'.

baseline_questions: Read: rain, play, cake. What sound do they share?
How many sounds are in 'ship'?
Read these tricky words: the, said, was, one.
Segment 'night' into sounds.
Write the /ai/ sound three different ways.
Underline the digraph: chin, thing, boat.

units.title: States of matter and the water cycle
units.subject: science
national_curriculum_refs: Sc4/3.1a compare and group materials together, according to whether they are solids, liquids or gases
Sc4/3.1b observe that some materials change state when they are heated or cooled, and measure or research the temperature at which this happens (°C)
Sc4/3.1c identify the part played by evaporation and condensation in the water cycle and associate the rate of evaporation with temperature
learning_objectives: Sort everyday materials into solids, liquids and gases by their properties
Describe melting and freezing as changes of state caused by heating or cooling
Measure temperature in degrees Celsius using a thermometer
Explain evaporation and condensation with everyday examples
Describe the water cycle using the words evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks a gas is not a material or 'not really there' because you often cannot see it.
misconceptions.why: Only visible, touchable things are counted as matter.
misconceptions.response: Trap air in a sealed bag or syringe and push on it; the air pushes back, so it is a material that takes up space.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks that when a puddle dries up the water has 'disappeared' or been destroyed.
misconceptions.why: Evaporation is invisible, so the water seems to vanish.
misconceptions.response: Cover a warm cup of water with a cold lid; watch droplets form. The water became a gas and then condensed back – it was never destroyed.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks steam and the bubbles in boiling water are 'air'.
misconceptions.why: Any gas is assumed to be air.
misconceptions.response: Explain the bubbles are water vapour (water as a gas); the visible cloud above is tiny droplets that have already condensed.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks condensation on a cold glass is water leaking through the glass.
misconceptions.why: No visible source, so it must come from inside.
misconceptions.response: Use a dry, sealed bottle of cold water; droplets still form on the outside – they come from water vapour in the air cooling down.

lessons.title: Putting it together: the water cycle

baseline_questions: Sort these into solid, liquid or gas: milk, a brick, the air in a balloon, sand, orange juice.
What is it called when a solid turns into a liquid? What causes it?
Water freezes at what temperature in °C?
Give one everyday example of evaporation and one of condensation.
Why do water droplets form on the outside of a cold drink?
Put the water cycle in order: condensation, evaporation, precipitation, collection.
A puddle disappears on a sunny day. Explain where the water has gone.

units.title: Rivers: what's special about them?
units.subject: geography
national_curriculum_refs: Ge2/1.3b describe and understand key aspects of physical geography, including rivers and the water cycle
Ge2/1.4a use maps, atlases, globes and digital mapping to locate countries and describe features studied
Ge2/1.4b use the eight points of a compass and locational language to describe features and routes
learning_objectives: Name the main features of a river: source, tributary, mouth, meander, bank
Describe how a river changes from its source to its mouth
Explain how rivers shape the land through erosion and deposition
Locate major UK rivers on a map (Thames, Severn, Trent)
Explain why flooding happens and some ways people manage it

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks a river's source is always a lake or the sea.
misconceptions.why: Rivers are seen only where they are large; the small start is overlooked.
misconceptions.response: Trace a real river on a map from a spring or hillside stream; the source is usually high ground, often just a trickle.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks rivers always flow from north to south (down the map).
misconceptions.why: 'Down' on a page is confused with downhill.
misconceptions.response: Show rivers flowing in every direction on a map; water flows from higher land to lower land, not from the top of the page.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks the water in a river is the same water sitting still, like a bath.
misconceptions.why: A river looks like a long pond.
misconceptions.response: Float a leaf on a stream; the water is always moving from source to mouth and is replaced by rain and tributaries.

baseline_questions: Label these river features: source, mouth, tributary, meander.
Where does a river usually start – high ground or low ground?
Name two rivers in the UK.
Explain one way a river changes the land as it flows.
Give one cause of river flooding and one way people try to reduce the damage.
True or false: rivers always flow from the top of a map to the bottom. Explain.

units.title: The Vikings: why did they come to Britain?
units.subject: history
national_curriculum_refs: Hi2/1.8 the Viking and Anglo-Saxon struggle for the Kingdom of England to the time of Edward the Confessor
Hi2/1.9a develop a chronologically secure knowledge and understanding of British history
Hi2/1.9c understand how our knowledge of the past is constructed from a range of sources
learning_objectives: Place the Viking period on a timeline in relation to the Romans and Anglo-Saxons
Give reasons why the Vikings left Scandinavia and came to Britain
Describe Viking raids and, later, Viking settlement
Explain how we know about the Vikings from archaeology and written sources
Explain that sources can be biased, e.g. accounts written by monks

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks the Vikings only ever raided and never settled or farmed.
misconceptions.why: The dramatic raid stories are the ones most often told.
misconceptions.response: Study place-name and excavation evidence (e.g. York/Jorvik); many Vikings farmed, traded and lived here for generations.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks 'the Vikings' were a single country or united army.
misconceptions.why: One label is taken to mean one group.
misconceptions.response: Map Scandinavia: Vikings came from areas that became Norway, Denmark and Sweden, in many separate groups.

misconceptions.misconception: Treats a monk's written account as simply 'what happened'.
misconceptions.why: Written = true; pupils don't yet weigh who wrote it and why.
misconceptions.response: Compare a monk's account of a raid with archaeological evidence; discuss why a victim of the raid might exaggerate.

misconceptions.misconception: Thinks all Vikings wore horned helmets.
misconceptions.why: A popular modern image repeated in cartoons.
misconceptions.response: There is no archaeological evidence for horned helmets in battle; show a real find (e.g. the Gjermundbu helmet).

prerequisites: Reading a timeline with BC/AD or BCE/CE

lessons.title: Who were the Vikings and where did they come from?
Why did the Vikings leave Scandinavia?
From raiding to settling: the Danelaw
How do we know about the Vikings?

baseline_questions: Put in order on a timeline: Romans, Anglo-Saxons, Vikings.
Give two reasons the Vikings came to Britain.
What is the difference between a raid and a settlement?
Name one type of evidence archaeologists use to learn about the Vikings.
A monk wrote that a Viking raid was 'the wrath of God'. Why might his account not be completely reliable?
True or false: all Vikings came from one country. Explain your answer.
